resources.string: Nodding saxifrage
Saxifraga cernua
bulbil saxifrage

A small Arctic–alpine perennial remarkable for axillary bulbils that allow vegetative reproduction. A solitary nodding white flower may appear above the basal leaves; the bulbils are often more conspicuous than the seed capsule.
Arctic and subarctic regions and high mountains of Eurasia and North America, on moist rocks and snow-bed margins.
Low perennial, usually 5–25 cm, with a basal rosette and one or a few flowering stems.
Basal leaves rounded to kidney-shaped and shallowly lobed; stem leaves may bear bulbils in their axils.
Usually a solitary, nodding, five-petalled white flower.
Small many-seeded capsule; axillary bulbils are an important means of spread.
Charlock mustard
Sinapis arvensis
wild mustard; charlock

An annual brassica of disturbed ground. Yellow four-petalled flowers and rough, lobed lower leaves help distinguish it from similar mustards; the fruit is a short-beaked silique. POWO treats the tree name as a synonym of Mutarda arvensis; this profile retains the tree label.
Native across much of Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia; now widespread in cultivated fields and disturbed ground.
Branched annual, commonly 20–100 cm tall.
Alternate leaves; lower blades lyrate and coarsely toothed, upper leaves narrower and less divided.
Yellow four-petalled flowers in terminal racemes.
Upright or spreading silique, often with a distinct beak.
Siamese cassia
Senna siamea
kassod tree; Cassia siamea

An evergreen tropical legume tree with many pairs of opposite leaflets and dense yellow flower clusters. Its long flat pods darken as they mature. It is often planted for shade, avenues and fuelwood; genus membership alone does not establish a food use.
Native to Sri Lanka and Indochina; widely planted in tropical regions.
Evergreen tree, often 8–20 m, with a rounded crown.
Alternate pinnate leaves bearing numerous opposite oblong leaflets.
Yellow five-petalled flowers in terminal or axillary racemes and panicles.
Long flattened legume, dark brown to black when mature.
Malay apple
Syzygium malaccense
mountain apple; Otaheite apple

A tropical evergreen myrtle recognizable by large opposite leaves and vivid clusters of pink-red flowers with very long stamens. The bell-shaped fruit is commonly eaten where cultivated; its colour ranges from pale pink to deep red.
Native from Malesia east into the Pacific; cultivated widely through the humid tropics.
Evergreen tree, commonly 8–18 m, with a dense crown.
Large opposite, simple, entire, elliptic to lance-shaped leaves.
Dense clusters on older branches; pink to crimson flowers have numerous long stamens.
Fleshy bell-shaped berry-like drupe, usually pink or red, with a single seed.
Mauritius national flower
Trochetia boutoniana
Trochetia; Ruizia boutoniana

A rare shrub endemic to Mauritius, famed for large carmine asymmetric flowers. The tree name is retained although POWO accepts Ruizia boutoniana and treats Trochetia boutoniana as its synonym. Its restricted wild occurrence makes precise locality claims best kept conservative.
Endemic to Mauritius; associated with the Le Morne area and cultivated in conservation collections.
Evergreen shrub or small tree, about 1.5–3 m.
Alternate simple ovate leaves with toothed margins.
Large axillary asymmetric deep carmine-red bell-like flowers.
Dry capsule that splits to release seeds.
Jamaican royal palm
Roystonea altissima
Jamaica royal palm

A tall solitary royal palm endemic to Jamaica. It has a smooth gray trunk, green crownshaft and large pinnate fronds; small flowers and dark fruits form branched clusters below the crown. It is distinct in range from Puerto Rican R. borinquena.
Endemic to Jamaica in wet tropical habitats; also cultivated as an ornamental palm.
Tall solitary palm, reported to reach roughly 25 m.
Large pinnate fronds with numerous narrow leaflets.
Small pale flowers in branched inflorescences below the crownshaft.
Small dark purple to black drupe in hanging clusters.
Guatemalan bromeliad
Hohenbergiopsis guatemalensis
Hohenbergiopsis

A large epiphytic tank bromeliad and the sole species of its genus. Broad strap-shaped leaves form a rosette that catches water; a stout central stalk bears a dense, branched, many-flowered inflorescence with overlapping bracts.
Southern Mexico (Oaxaca and Chiapas) to Guatemala, in humid forest.
Epiphytic rosette about 50–70 cm tall in flower; leaves may exceed 1 m.
Numerous broad strap-shaped leaves form a rosette with spinose-serrate margins and sheathing bases.
Dense compound inflorescence with many tightly arranged flowers, purple petals and conspicuous bracts.
Fleshy berry containing seeds.
Creeping feather-moss
Amblystegium serpens
creeping moss

A small pleurocarpous moss forming delicate mats on bark, soil and stone. Tiny narrow leaves and curved capsules on reddish setae are useful field characters, but species-level identification often needs microscopic examination.
Widespread in temperate regions on damp soil, stone, tree bases and other shaded substrates.
Very small creeping moss, forming low mats only a few centimetres high.
Tiny narrow lance-shaped leaves along creeping irregularly branched shoots.
No flowers; moss reproductive organs are borne on the gametophyte.
Curved ovoid capsule on a slender reddish seta; sporophytes may be absent.
Androy tree
Androya decaryi
Androya

A small tree endemic to southern Madagascar and the only species of Androya. Opposite narrow, often slightly falcate leaves with three basal veins help identify sterile material; its small white subrotate flowers have four stamens.
Known from southern Madagascar between the Toliara and Fort-Dauphin regions, in dry environments.
Small tree about 3–10 m tall.
Opposite narrow leathery leaves, often slightly sickle-shaped, with three basal veins.
Small white, almost wheel-shaped corolla with four stamens.
Ovoid capsule.
Golden drops
Onosma echioides
golden drop; Onosma

A bristly perennial of rocky grassland and open slopes. It forms a basal rosette and coiled flowering shoots bearing nodding yellow tubular flowers, a typical Boraginaceae pattern. Its dense stiff hairs are conspicuous.
Native from Sicily through the Balkans and parts of southeastern Europe, in dry rocky habitats.
Low perennial herb, roughly 10–50 cm, with erect flowering stems.
Basal and stem leaves lance-shaped and covered with stiff bristles.
Nodding tubular yellow flowers in coiled clusters.
Four small nutlets develop within the persistent calyx.
Bacigalupi’s downingia
Downingia bacigalupii
Bach’s calicoflower

A delicate annual of seasonal wetlands. Its blue bilaterally symmetrical flower is diagnostic: two smaller upper lobes and a broad three-lobed lower lip with paired yellow marks edged in white. It flowers in vernal pools while soil moisture persists.
Western North America, especially California and adjacent states, in vernal pools and wet grassland.
Slender branching annual, usually about 5–35 cm.
Small alternate, narrow to diamond-shaped stem leaves.
Blue to violet bilaterally symmetrical flower with two yellow-white marks on the lower lip.
Slender dehiscent capsule with numerous small seeds.
Allthorn
Koeberlinia spinosa
crown of thorns; allthorn

A highly branched desert shrub whose green twigs end in rigid spines; true leaves are minute and soon shed. Tiny greenish-white four-part flowers are followed by glossy black fruits. Its spiny silhouette is more diagnostic than its inconspicuous leaves.
Arid and semi-arid southwestern United States and northern Mexico.
Compact spreading shrub or small tree, 0.5–10 m depending on variety and conditions.
Leaves minute, narrow and soon deciduous; green branchlets become spine-tipped.
Tiny greenish-white flowers with four sepals and four petals.
Small shiny black berry-like fruit, tipped by the persistent style.
Thick-leaved groundcherry
Physalis crassifolia
yellow nightshade groundcherry

A low perennial groundcherry of dry western North American habitats. Its nodding yellow flower has dark markings near the throat; after flowering the inflated, veined calyx encloses a berry. Do not eat it based on resemblance to cultivated edible Physalis.
Southwestern United States to northwestern Mexico, in dry open places.
Low perennial herb, often sprawling or ascending, about 10–60 cm.
Alternate ovate to lance-ovate leaves, relatively thick, with toothed or wavy margins.
Nodding yellow five-lobed flower with dark brown-purple markings at the base.
Berry enclosed by an inflated, veined papery calyx; edibility is not asserted.
Quipá cactus
Tacinga inamoena
quipá; Opuntia inamoena

A low Brazilian cactus of the Caatinga, with flattened oval to obovate cladodes and numerous tiny glochids in nearly unarmed areoles. Orange-red flowers have reflexed tepals; mature fruits are yellow to orange. Glochids detach easily and irritate skin.
Endemic to northeastern Brazil and northern Minas Gerais, in Caatinga, rocky fields and exposed outcrops.
Decumbent subshrub, usually 20–30 cm tall.
True leaves are short-lived; flattened oval cladodes bear areoles with fine golden to brown glochids.
Orange-red flower with reflexed perianth segments.
Globose fleshy fruit, green when immature and yellow to orange at maturity.
Blue Turk’s-cap cactus
Melocactus azureus
blue Melocactus

A distinctive globular cactus with a blue-green waxy stem and a terminal reddish cephalium of dense wool and bristles. Tiny magenta flowers and narrow pinkish fruits emerge from the cephalium; ordinary stem growth does not continue above it.
Endemic to Bahia, northeastern Brazil, in dry rocky Caatinga habitats.
Globose cactus about 10–40 cm tall; the cephalium develops on mature plants.
No true leaves; the blue-green ribbed stem bears areoles with stout spines.
Small magenta flowers emerge from the terminal cephalium.
Elongated narrow pink to whitish berry arising from the cephalium.
Chain cactus
Rhipsalis paradoxa
coral cactus; mistletoe cactus

An epiphytic cactus with long hanging chains of flattened, three-winged segments joined in a characteristic zigzag. Small white flowers appear near the tips, followed by pale berry-like fruits. It is leafless: its photosynthetic structures are segmented stems.
Native to humid Atlantic forests of southeastern Brazil; commonly grown as an epiphyte.
Freely branching and pendent, with chains that may exceed 1 m.
No true leaves; flattened three-angled stem segments repeat in a zigzag.
Small white subterminal flowers, around 2 cm.
Small pale pinkish-white berry.
Dinner-plate tree
Pterospermum acerifolium
kanak champa; maple-leaved bayur

A large Asian tree whose striking leaves range from entire to maple-lobed and have a brown velvety underside. Large fragrant white flowers have five petals and hairy sepals; its woody capsule opens to release winged seeds. Leaf shape varies on the same tree.
Native from the Indian subcontinent through mainland Southeast Asia; grown as an ornamental and shade tree.
Large evergreen or briefly deciduous tree, often 15–30 m.
Very large alternate leaves, entire to palmately lobed, with a densely brown-tomentose underside.
Large fragrant white flowers, usually solitary or few, with five petals and hairy sepals.
Large woody capsule splitting into valves; seeds bear long wings.
Jetbead
Rhodotypos scandens
black jetbead; white kerria

A deciduous East Asian rose-family shrub. Opposite strongly veined, double-toothed leaves and four-petalled white flowers distinguish it from many ornamental roses. Each flower develops one to four glossy black drupelets on a small receptacle.
Native to China, Korea and Japan; also planted and naturalized elsewhere.
Upright arching shrub, about 1–2 m tall.
Opposite ovate leaves with prominent veins and sharply double-serrate margins.
White flower with exactly four petals and numerous stamens.
One to four glossy black drupelets grouped on the receptacle.
Water apple
Syzygium aqueum
watery rose apple; wax apple

A tropical evergreen tree grown for its crisp, watery, bell-shaped fruit. Opposite lance-shaped leaves accompany clusters of white flowers with long pink-tipped stamens. The fruit ranges from white to pink or red; this species differs from the larger-fruited Malay apple, S. malaccense.
Native from Malesia to the western Pacific; cultivated widely in tropical Asia.
Small to medium evergreen tree, commonly 5–10 m.
Opposite simple lanceolate leaves with entire margins.
Clusters of white flowers with many long stamens, often pinkish at their tips.
Bell-shaped waxy juicy berry-like fruit, commonly white to pink or red.
Hairy-rachis yellow flame tree
Peltophorum dasyrhachis
Peltophorum dasyrhachis

A spreading tropical Asian legume tree with finely divided bipinnate leaves and hanging yellow flower clusters. The inflorescence axis is characteristically reddish and hairy; flattened pods with a narrow winged edge mark fruiting branches.
Native from southern China through mainland Southeast Asia and Malesia; cultivated as a shade tree.
Large spreading tree, often 10–25 m.
Alternate bipinnate leaves with many small paired leaflets.
Pendant yellow racemes or panicles on reddish hairy axes.
Flattened oblong pod with a narrow wing-like margin and pointed tip.
